title: Three to Four Cups of Coffee a Day Can Halve Your Risk of Liver Cancer — and Decaf Works Too
excerpt: A 354,957-person Cedars-Sinai study finds that moderate coffee drinking — regular or decaf — is linked to dramatically lower rates of cirrhosis, liver cancer and liver-related death, with implications for South Asians facing rising fatty liver disease
body:
India runs on chai, but it may be time to make room for coffee. A landmark study tracking 354,957 adults over 13 years has found that drinking three to four cups of coffee a day is associated with a 49 per cent lower risk of developing liver cancer and a 32 per cent lower risk of cirrhosis — the scarring that turns a healthy liver into a failing one.

The findings, published this week in *Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology* by researchers at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles, represent the most comprehensive assessment to date of long-term coffee consumption and liver health.

## The Numbers Are Hard to Ignore

Lead author Dr Hyunseok Kim, a transplant hepatologist at Cedars-Sinai, and his team used advanced MRI imaging alongside clinical data to build a three-layered picture of how coffee affects the liver. Coffee drinkers had less fat in and around their liver, lower inflammation markers and healthier liver protein profiles — all of which aligned with the reduced clinical outcomes.

The dose-response curve was striking. Even one to two cups a day were associated with a 20 per cent lower risk of cirrhosis and a 24 per cent lower risk of liver cancer. At five or more cups, the risk reductions climbed to 32 per cent for cirrhosis, 47 per cent for liver cancer and 42 per cent for liver-related death.

Perhaps most surprisingly, decaffeinated coffee showed similar protective effects. The antioxidant compounds in coffee — polyphenols, chlorogenic acids and diterpenes — survive the decaffeination process and appear to be doing the heavy lifting rather than caffeine itself.

> **""We would not recommend that someone begin drinking coffee solely for liver protection based on this study alone," he said."**

"When the imaging and the proteins line up with the clinical outcomes, the overall picture becomes more believable than any one measure would be alone," said Lauren Manaker, a registered dietitian nutritionist who was not involved in the study.

## Why This Matters for South Asians

![Los Angeles — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5a/Hollywood_Sign_%28Zuschnitt%29.jpg/3840px-Hollywood_Sign_%28Zuschnitt%29.jpg)

Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease has become a silent epidemic among South Asians, both in India and across the diaspora. Studies estimate that 30 to 40 per cent of urban Indians now have some form of NAFLD — driven by a combination of genetic susceptibility, visceral fat distribution, insulin resistance and increasingly sedentary lifestyles. Among Indian Americans, the prevalence may be even higher because of dietary shifts toward processed and high-sugar foods after immigration.

Fatty liver disease progresses through a spectrum: fat accumulation, inflammation, fibrosis and eventually cirrhosis or liver cancer. The coffee study suggests that moderate consumption may intervene at multiple points in this cascade by reducing liver fat, dampening inflammation and supporting healthier liver protein activity.

India's coffee culture, particularly strong in the south, offers a natural dietary entry point. Filter coffee — the thick, chicory-blended brew beloved in Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Kerala — is traditionally served in moderate quantities, aligning with the study's three-to-four-cup sweet spot. For diaspora Indians in the US, UK and Canada who have adopted daily coffee habits, the study provides welcome evidence that the ritual may be doing their liver real favours.

## The Caveats

Senior author Dr Ju Dong Yang, medical director of the Liver Cancer Program at Cedars-Sinai, urged caution about extrapolating too far. "We would not recommend that someone begin drinking coffee solely for liver protection based on this study alone," he said. "Prevention should continue to focus on maintaining a healthy weight, limiting alcohol, exercising regularly, and managing blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol."

The study also found that participants who sweetened their coffee with sugar or artificial substitutes had an elevated marker for liver inflammation — a reminder that loading your cup with syrup and processed creamers can undermine the benefits. The US FDA recommends limiting caffeine intake to no more than 400 milligrams a day, roughly two to three 12-ounce cups, and stopping at least six hours before bedtime to avoid sleep disruption.

More than 90 per cent of participants were European, so the findings need validation across diverse ethnic groups. But the sheer scale of the study and its multi-layered methodology — combining clinical outcomes with imaging and biomarker data — makes it one of the strongest pieces of evidence yet for coffee's hepatoprotective effects.

## The Bottom Line

For the millions of NRIs who already drink coffee daily, this study is a quiet validation: your morning cup is almost certainly doing your liver some good. For those dealing with early-stage fatty liver disease, moderate black coffee — minus the sugar and cream — may be one of the simplest dietary interventions available. And for the chai loyalists willing to experiment, a cup or two of coffee alongside your regular routine is unlikely to hurt and may help protect one of the body's most vital organs.
